note.question: Does more accurate consumer targeting always help advertisers, or can it make competition so intense that firms should target different groups or shrink their product portfolios?
note.overview: Two firms strategically choose which valuation segment to target and whom to message before competing in price. The paper fully characterizes subgame-perfect Nash equilibria, including endogenous segmentation and mixed pricing when both firms chase high-value consumers.

models.method: The authors solve the pricing subgame conditional on first-stage targeting and reach, compare deviation profits to identify SPNE regions, prove nonmonotonic comparative statics in signal accuracy, and extend the game to endogenous product count, broad appeal, alternative timing, and publisher-mediated advertising.

components.label: Model sequence and system structure
components.explanation: In stage one, each firm chooses the consumer group it targets and which noisy-signal recipients receive an ad. After observing those choices, firms simultaneously set prices. Consumers who receive relevant messages observe prices and buy at the lowest available price. Extensions allow simultaneous timing, multiple products, broader product appeal, and ads purchased from two publishers.

components.label: Subgame-perfect Nash equilibrium in targeting, message reach, and pricing
components.explanation: The model's equilibrium concept is Subgame-perfect Nash equilibrium in targeting, message reach, and pricing. Section 3.1 explicitly adopts SPNE. Lemmas 1-2 characterize pure targeting and mixed pricing for high and zero advertising cost; Propositions 1-7 extend the nonmonotone profit and segmentation results across costs, products, timings, appeal, and publishers.
